title: Confidence Interval Laboratory
summary: Two staged experiments. In the first, a simulated population has a true mean the studies never see, and repeated samples produce a stack of confidence intervals whose misses are marked, so coverage can be counted rather than asserted; sample size and variability change the width of those intervals and leave the coverage alone. In the second, four fictional trials are judged one at a time against a threshold of practical importance that the learner sets, which makes a precise trivial finding and a wide uninformative one look as different as they are. A select-all challenge then works through the standard misreadings of a 95% interval.
learningObjectives: State what the 95% in a 95% confidence interval is a property of, and why it is not a probability about the interval on screen.
Distinguish the width of an interval from the coverage of the procedure that produced it.
Explain why sample size changes precision but not long-run coverage, and why the confidence level changes both.
Judge a reported interval against a stated threshold of practical importance rather than against zero alone.
Recognise that a wide interval containing zero is an inconclusive study rather than evidence of no effect.
interactionTypes: judging fictional claims against a threshold the learner sets
privacy: No data collected, stored or transmitted; every sample is generated in the browser tab, and the tool asks nothing about the person using it.
accessibilityNotes: Native ranges, a select, a number input, radio groups, checkboxes and buttons, each with an explicit label and grouped in a fieldset with a legend; every slider announces a meaningful value such as '25 participants in each study'. Both charts are hidden from assistive technology and paired inside their figures with visible tables - a two-row outcome table for the caterpillar plot and a four-row quantity table for the single-claim picture - and a disclosure lists the ten most recent studies row by row. Intervals that missed the true mean are dashed and carry a cross drawn at the true value, so a miss is marked by shape as well as by colour; the band of changes worth having carries a diagonal hatch as well as a tint and is labelled in words. Each experiment keeps one pinned primary result under 470px tall so the controls beside it stay usable inside a 768px-tall viewport. Every action announces a full sentence through the polite live region, focus moves to the Experiment 1 heading when it opens, forced-colours rules are provided, and the layout is usable at 320px and at classroom-projector widths with no horizontal page scroll.
readmeTopic: Coverage is a property of the procedure: count the misses, then separate precision from importance
simulationNotes: Experiment 1 draws n observations from Normal(12, sigma) - a fictional mean change of 12.0 minutes of walking per day - and reports the sample mean plus or minus z(level) times sigma over the square root of n, with z taken from a fixed table of normal quantiles at 80, 90, 95 and 99 per cent. Sigma is treated as known because the simulation states it, which is why the multiplier is a normal rather than a t quantile; a real study estimates sigma from its own sample and uses t, which widens the interval at small n, and the page says so in its limitations. Because sigma is known every interval in a run has the same width, so the only thing that varies from study to study is where the interval sits - the picture then shows the intervals moving around a truth that does not. Nominal coverage is exact under this model, so changing n or sigma changes width while only the confidence level changes coverage. Randomness is seeded with mulberry32 and Box-Muller normals, and changing any design setting clears the pile because those studies came from a different procedure. Experiment 2 uses four invented trials with fixed reported means and 95% intervals, chosen to occupy the four corners of the precision-by-importance space; the correct classification is computed from the learner's own threshold, so moving the threshold changes the correct verdict without any datum changing. No real study, participant, application or dataset is involved.
